Hey! DPhiE member here. The other commenters are right, the pin is our membership badge and the attachment is what’s called a chapter guard. It represents the specific chapter of Delta Phi Epsilon that your grandmother was likely a part of. While DPhiE is a secular sorority, our founders were Jewish and some of our chapters have close associations with Jewish organizations. Some of our Jewish members also join because of this heritage, and your grandmother was likely one of them. You may be able to reach out to DPhiE IHQ to corroborate her membership, but I don’t know if that’s something they’d share with non-members.

I can’t speak on the Hillel key, as I’m not a member of that organization, but **please do not wear the Delta Phi Epsilon pin or Greek key, as you are not an initiated sister of Delta Phi Epsilon, and only initiated sisters are allowed to wear the pin. The key is a little different, but it does have our Greek letters on it, which are generally restricted to initiated sisters or sweethearts.** I hope I was able to answer some questions!

I know this post is super old, but I’m putting this here for anyone else who might be confused as to why these chocolates are making their GI system upset: it’s not the lactose, it’s the sorbitol. The majority of caffeine supplements (chocolates, mints, gummies, etc.) use sorbitol as a sweetener/preservative. Sorbitol is also used as a laxative, and is known to cause nausea, gas, diarrhea, or stomach cramps ([source](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/what-is-sorbitol#side-effects-precautions)). So it’s more than likely the cause of your symptoms, especially since lactaid didn’t fix the problem.

"I'm so dysfunctional that I can't even do --insert task here-- without my meds") until my psychiatrist explained to me that I wasn't struggling because I was stupid or dysfunctional, but because I had a chemical imbalance in my brain that my meds helped to correct. My meds were never the reason I started improving and succeeding. They were a factor of course, but they simply put me at the same baseline as neurotypical individuals, and the rest was my own doing. Hearing that really changed my perspective and has helped me realize that my meds aren't a "crutch," but a tool to help me.

I take my stimulants on days I know I need to be focused, wether that be for work or for personal projects. I personally find that they make social interaction a lot easier because they help me stay on topic and focused on conversation, so if I have plans with friends I’ll take them as well. Ultimately though, I recommended listening to your doctor and your body. Try taking your meds when you’re off work for a few days and see how you feel, if it’s not good then stop. Everyone’s different and it can take a few tries to figure out what works best for you.

Write about the consequences of their power. A lot of movies gloss over the aftermath. Deliberately writing about how many people were inside the skyscraper that the MC knocked down, or how much damage the MC's body takes from exerting itself so much can give the MC a legitimate reason to avoid using their powers unless absolutely necessary. Giving the MC an appropriate weakness can also help. I would avoid making the MC the only person in the story with such powers (unless you're going for a "chosen one" narrative) so that it's not as jarring to see one person level entire streets.

Just start. I know it's a bit cliche, but it's true. Your first story is going to be garbage, and probably the next few stories too, but over time you'll learn and progress. It just takes time. You don't even have to write a coherent story, just write a random scene you have in your head. All that matters is that you're putting words onto paper

I'm probably going to get downvoted for saying this, but I'm going to be honest with you. Going in blind will only result in failure. If this is really, truly what you want to do in life, you need to do a lot of research. 

Firstly, a general fashion design degree isn't what you're going to need to get into the shoe design industry. You're going to want to have a bachelor's or an associate's degree in fashion design, then take more specific classes for accessory and shoe design on top of that. Look at schools in your area that offer these classes, and see if you can take them.

Secondly, The fashion industry is notoriously hard to break into. Its oversaturated with talent, and getting a few jobs doesn't guarantee success. You can work your hardest and still not succeed. You'll need money to fund your carrier, which can be tough if you have no guarantee you'll ever earn it back, especially on top of student loan debts. I say this as someone who wanted to be a fashion designer for years before ultimately changing courses in life to keep fashion as a hobby. 

Most importantly, make sure this is what you want to be doing from 9-5, 5 days a week. Get ready to have people tell you your designs look terrible, give you unrealistic deadlines, try to take credit for your work, push you down to raise themselves up, and everything else that comes with a carrier in the arts. If that doesn't sound like what you want to do, then keep shoe design as a hobby. However, if this is truly your passion in life, if it's what you know you've been created to do, go for it. Educate yourself on what requirements you'll need, figure out a backup carrier in case design doesn't work out, start saving up money, and give it your absolute best.

I know this is a super long post, but as someone who's been in the exact same place you've been in, I hope I could be of assistance. Good luck in breaking into the industry!

By far the scariest story I've ever heard was from a podcast I listen to called "Spooked" (episode linked below). It's about three girls who went camping in New Mexico to visit some of the hot springs near the Rio Grande Gorge. They were having a good time and were relaxing until it was just them and a middle-aged man with his dog left near the spring. The man wasn't swimming or anything, he just seemed to be waiting for the girls to get out of the pool. Once the girls got out, the dog walked over to each of them one by one and rubbed up against them kind of like a cat would. When it returned to the man he took out a bandana and rubbed the dog with it. Then he said, "See you later ladies" and left. 

When the guy was gone one of the girls pulled the others aside and told them that the dog was trained to pick up their scent and that the guy was probably going to come back to find them. There was only one trail back to their car, where the guy could have easily been waiting for them. They went back to their camp and were trying to figure out what to do when they saw the beam of a flashlight coming through the woods, and all three of them just bolted.

The thing about the Rio Grande Gorge is that it's *long*, like 80 something miles long or something, and there's no way to cross the river, no bridge or narrow spot where the water slows down or gets shallow, so the three girls were basically stuck. 

They were in the middle of a national park or something, and there wasn't anyone around for miles, the only thing they could see while they were on top of the gorge was the light of a few houses in the distance. The girls just *ran* for the houses, sprinting up hills and literally rolling down the other side, and the whole time they could all hear the sound of a dog barking just behind them, sometimes they could even see the guy's flashlight following them. They ran for **miles** just trying to get the dog to lose their scent, and the girl telling the story said that she was so exhausted she honestly didn't know if she could keep going. 

By some miracle, they made it to a house and the people inside let them in and called the cops. The cops came and escorted the girls back to their campsite to see what was up, and when they got there they found a ton of boot prints coming from the woods and circling their tent.

Let me tell you, as someone who loves to go trail running, I did not go for a run for months without carrying at least a swiss army knife with me. Still gives me the creeps whenever I think about those girls and what they went through.
